    “It is okay,” Kate felt Yelena shrug against her. “You are well within your rights to think that way.”

    “Am I? I don’t know, I just feel like I’m objectifying you in a way that you don’t want to be objectified. It feels like I’m violating your-”

    “Hey,” Yelena forced Kate to meet her eyes again. “This,” a gloved hand found hers and placed it gently against Yelena’s chest. “This is for you to think about in whatever way you want. You have my permission, okay?”

    Kate had to tear her eyes away from her maybe-girlfriend's loving look. It was so hard to hold her gaze, when she looked at Kate in that way, with such intensity, and so much feeling. “Okay,” she whispered, and felt compelled to add a, “Thanks” a moment later. Wow, she was a dork.

    “But er,” Yelena sniffed a little, at the cold and worked her hands up and over Kate’s thighs to try and generate some heat. “I probably won’t want to. I don’t know if I will ever want to, you know, receive.”

    “And that’s my compromise,” Kate explained, with absolute certainty, as her eyes snapped back to Yelena’s. “Because you are completely and utterly worth it. Please remember that”. And this was the key, this was Kate’s job, to make Yelena feel worth it. She had to comfort her in other ways, pleasure her in other ways, love her in other ways, so it could never be in doubt that Kate Bishop loved Yelena Belova.

    Yelena nodded. “I will try”. The brunette raised a mightily unimpressed eyebrow and the blonde quickly corrected herself. “I will try, very hard.”

    “Good. And I really want you to do me too, I think about it all the time.”

    “I know,” Yelena smiled, warmly. Of course she knew.

    “When you’re in your uniform. When you’re in the gym. When you’re cooking in the kitchen. When you speak Russian. Oh god.” She could feel Yelena chuckle a little against her. This was the most honest she’d ever been about this, and it felt fantastic. She didn’t need it to end up with Yelena actually following through, she just needed get it off of her chest, where it was sitting so heavy. “Sometimes I want it to be slow, intimate and meaningful and I just want your hands and your mouth on me. I want to come with you inside of me.”

    Yelena blinked. “Wow.” Shit, did I go too far? I went too far.

    “Too much?” Kate asked, anxiously, but Yelena was quick to alleviate her fears.

    “No, no, I-I asked for honesty. I guess sometimes I just think of sex as something people do to get off. Sometimes I forget that it can be other things too.”

    “Okay good, because other times, I do just want you to rail me.”

    The blonde frowned. “Rail you? I’m not familiar with-”

    “Yeah, it kind of means, like… rough.”

    “You want me to be rough with you?” Yelena asked. Kate couldn’t tell whether her maybe- girlfriend was seeking clarity or whether she was a little taken aback.

    “Oh god,” Kate groaned, and once again she pressed herself against Yelena in a vain attempt to disappear entirely. Maybe Yelena had been right, maybe Kate did say inane things. But then again, if you couldn’t tell your devuskhka these things, who could you tell them to?

    “Well, that is good to know,” Yelena said, as she pulled Kate into her. “It certainly plays into my skillset so it is not the craziest thing I have ever heard.”

    Kate could only laugh. “How are you making this so easy?”

    Yelena shrugged. “Well, sex intimidates me, sure. Talking about what I want and my sexuality can be scary. But sex does not embarrass me. How can it embarrass me if I have never cared about it? And why should you be embarrassed about what you want? I don’t want you to feel ashamed of what you want ever again, and if I make you feel that way, you have permission to attempt to kick my ass.”

    There was a moment of silence before Kate whispered a quiet, “Thank you,” and placed another soft kiss upon Yelena’s neck. It felt right, it all did. Despite the cold, and the wind and the snow, they felt like they were exactly where they needed to be, in each other’s arms. But it would soon be time to head back to the homestead. The early midwinter evening was drawing in, and despite Yelena’s impeccable survival skills, she didn’t fancy the walk back in the snow. She also didn’t want to risk Clint mounting a search party, after fearing Yelena had murdered Kate, and finding them this way.

    “So...” Kate began slowly.

    “Mhmm,” came Yelena’s comfortable response.

    “In summary, avoid below the belt, anything above is fair game.”

    “Yes.”

    “And if you change your mind that’s totally fine. At any time. Even during, especially during.” Because consent was key, and could be retracted at any time.

    “Okay.”

    “I can still touch your butt though, right?”

    “Yes.”

    “Good,’ Kate sighed, happily, “Because I really like your butt.”

    “I know,” Yelena said, smugly, and she had the right, because she really did have an incredible butt.

    “Thank you, for doing this,” Kate continued. She really did mean it. “I know that you’re worried but so many couples have sex but never get what they want from each other. Like comfort and companionship, trust and love.” Yelena raised her eyebrow at the L word and Kate simply rolled her eyes. “I know you’re not ready for the love bit, and that’s cool but I do feel whatever it is that you hold for me, every day. I hope you feel mine for you."

    “I do, I feel it,” Yelena nodded, with the sincerest of smiles.

    “Just you talking to me about this, do you know how much that means to me? Do you know how much that says about us and you especially?” Kated asked, hands either side of Yelena’s happy face, their eyes locked together. “There’s a part of me that is still hurt and still angry. When you feel those feelings, they can’t just be magicked away, I guess, but we can move forward. I can forgive you if you can forgive me for pushing? I’m just…” Kate sighed and laughed, self-deprecatingly. “I’m just fuckin head over heels, man.”

    Yelena grinned. Kate had the tiniest of hunches that Yelena felt the same way. “I forgive you,” the Russian said, earnestly.

    “Good. We should do this again. Preferably indoors and with wine or something?”

    “This talk?” Yelena asked.

    “Yeah. If we feel we need it, we should talk.” Kate wasn’t wrong. She knew things weren’t always going to be plain sailing with Yelena, that’s what happened when both people entered a relationship with more baggage than an Airbus a321, that and they were both superheroes for a living which came with its own stresses. “You said that we were on a journey but on different paths or… something?”

    Yelena cringed, “I did say that awful thing, yes.”

    “Then we should probably have a few regular check ins don’t you think? Just to make sure we’re still heading in the same direction.” It was sounding more and more sensible the more Kate thought about it.

    “Sure. As long as there is alcohol involved. Oh, and food would be good.” Incredibly sensible.

    “Food would be amazing,” Kate nodded her enthusiasm for their ingenious plan. “Oh, and for the record, I know this is way off but I think you should know, I don’t want to be your wife.”

    To her credit, Yelena didn’t miss a bit, despite the curve ball. “What?! No, I have always wanted a wife. It is over between us! I can’t.”

    Kate grinned at her idiocy. “I just don’t really want the whole marriage thing. I actually kind of like engagements more than marriages come to think of it.”

    “Really?”

    “Yeah. You know, an engagement is personal. It’s private and special, and beautiful and it’s just two people saying they want to spend the rest of their lives with each other. A marriage is an expensive day to sign some papers in front of a tonne of people who aren’t part of the relationship. And you have to pay for their food.”

    “If I got married and had to pay for everyone’s food, I would be minesweeping every fucking table for leftovers. I would have zero shame. Either that or a zero-tolerance policy on leaving any part of the meal.” The brunette couldn’t help but laugh as Yelena continued. “Marriage is fucking dumb for sure. Just add it to the very long list of ways men like to subjugate women.”

    “Amen.”

    “Although,” Yelena said, in such a way that captured Kate’s attention. “I don’t mind older ceremonies so much. Like hand fasting.”

    Well, well, well, wasn’t Yelena Belova full of surprises. “Really?”

    “Yeah, it is kind of cool right? And Russian weddings can be so long. Oh my god, they go on for days. Just get a rope, tie two people together, start a fire and get drunk. I like it. The pagans, they are smart, efficient people.”

    “That does sound like more your thing,” Kate said, with a smirk.

    Yelena narrowed her eyes, menacingly. “What are you suggesting?”

    “That you like arson, drinking and tying people up. In that order.”

    The blonde rolled her eyes dramatically. “Pfft. I do not think you know me at all, Kate Bishop.”

    “I know you better than you think.”

    “Oh really?” Yelena asked, eyebrow raised. “If that were true then you would know I like drinking above all. Tying people up is a close second,” she quipped with a wink and a grin.

    It was Kate’s turn to roll her eyes, as she slapped the back of her hands against Yelena’s stomach once more. “Flirt.”

    “I would tie you up if it would keep you safe. I would gag you if it meant you would stop asking people to stab you.”

    Kate cringed. “You are never going to let me live that down.”

    “I will if you promise not to do it again”. Yelena’s face was sterner now, but she was still smiling, warmly. She couldn’t resist the Kate Biship charm.

    “I can’t make those kinds of promises,” Kate said, as Yelena groaned in displeasure. “Okay, okay, I won’t ask anyone to stab me again.” Except maybe you.

    “Good, because I need you to remember that you are human. You are a very talented human being, but you are still human and you might die if you are stabbed.”

    “I know that,” Kate said as she shrugged off her maybe-girlfriend's concern.

    “Do you?” Yelena asked. Her hands gripped Kate’s hips, firmly, and something in her eyes wiped the smiled from Kate’s face.

    “Yes,” she said, meekly.

    “I am being serious.” Yelena stressed; emotion evident in her voice. “If we are committing to a future together, that means you committing to trying to be around for it.” The blonde had a point, but she was also forgetting the fact that they were superheroes, these weren’t exactly things either of them could commit to.

    “But what if there’s going to be a nuclear explosion and the only way for me to save New York City is for me to fly a nuclear warhead into a wormhole?”

    Yelena’s face did little to hide the fact that she wasn’t particularly impressed with Kate’s response. “I feel like these are exceptional circumstances.”

    “But not completely impossible circumstances.” Kate knew that she was now being contrary, but of course Yelena was showing her usual patience, a patience she only held for Kate.

    “True. But I would classify that risk as necessary under the job description of ‘Superhero’. Asking someone to stab you is an unnecessary risk and is really just super dumb.”

    Kate couldn’t keep the grin from her face. She knew it was idiotic at the time, and she knew it was her fault it happened, and she knew that if she wanted Yelena to feel comfortable with having her back out in the field again, then she really would have to admit her mistake. Suck it up, Kate. You can do it. “It is really dumb.”

    “Yes!” Yelena practically screamed in catharsis.

    “It still really hurts.”

    “Jesus,” Yelena shook her head and smiled disbelievingly.

    “Hey! I’ve learned my lesson.” And she really had, Kate did not want to be stabbed again.

    “I hope so because I am not burying you.” Yelena’s tone was light, but she knew that the Russian was deadly serious. Kate had no intention of burying the woman she loved either, no intention whatsoever.

    “So, I have to bury you?” Kate asked, that seemed a little unfair.

    “I am older,” Yelena shrugged, simply, and Kate raised a roguish eyebrow.

    “So, we’re getting old together?”

    “I did not say that,” Yelena chided, but there was no way that Kate could miss the twinkle in her maybe-girlfriend's eyes.

    Kate and Yelena returned, just as night was falling. The young brunette had made every attempt to open the door to the homestead oh so quietly, but it was no use, the Bartons were ready for them.

    “Kate, where have you been?” Clint questioned her as soon as she was across the threshold, concerned plastered across his face as he pulled her into a fierce hug. “I was about to head out there to look for you.”

    “I’m fine, we’re fine.” Kate said, as she gently extracted herself from his embrace.

    “Hey, you two had a good walk?” Laura asked. Momma Barton was clearly less concerned about Kate and Yelena’s well-being, which came as no surprise to Kate.

    “Good, it was good. Thank you,” Kate beamed. She was happy, incredibly happy. She would be even happier if Laura answered her next question in the way that she was hoping for. Kate glanced at Yelena who sent a small, reassuring smile her way, as smile that didn’t go unnoticed by Laura.

    “Will you be staying, Yelena?” Laura inquired. As it turned, out Kate didn’t even need to ask if Yelena could stay for the holidays. “There’s more than enough room at the inn, and we seem to have prepared a meal that would feed the five thousand.” Kate felt giddy. Her life really was making a habit of turning itself on itself within just a few hours. As eventful as it was, Kate hoped that maybe she could at least now enjoy a period of relative normalcy and stability.

    Yelena shuffled a little awkwardly and eyed Clint who gave her a resolute smile. It was small, but it was there. Kate suspected that Laura had had a word whilst they’d been out. He was stubborn and protective but it was only because he loved so fiercely, and Kate would always be able to forgive him for that. To Kate’s surprise, Yelena smiled back and then thanked the Bartons for the offer, one that she gladly accepted.

    Within moments their sodden boots were off, and their coats were hung next to the door. Both were ushered into the lounge where the fire now licked and roared. Kate could feel the heat begin to infiltrate her body, as it soothed her cold hands and joints. Hot cups of cocoa were unceremoniously forced upon them, as Laura wasn’t taking no for an answer, and Clint had been sent upstairs to find Yelena a ugly Christmas sweater to wear, much to her chagrin. Kate was pretty impressed by how well Yelena had hidden her disgust at the suggestion that she remove her thick, black woollen jumper and replace it with a thin, synthetic piece of holiday tat.

    "Yelena, this is Cooper, my eldest.”

    “Hi,” Coops smiled and nodded politely and Yelena waved a little awkwardly. This was probably a lot for her.

    “His sister Lila,” Laura continued as Lila smiled enthusiastically.

    “Hey! You kicked my dad’s butt, right?” She asked, mischievously.

    “Only because I let her!” Bellowed Clint, from upstairs. Was his hearing aid set to eleven or something? Wow.

    “We will let him think that,” Yelena whispered, conspiratorially, “Better for his ego.” Lila smiled and Kate realised that she had some serious best big sister competition in Yelena Belova. Yelena Belova was cool, way cooler than Kate.

    “And this is Nate,” Laura continued, “He’s quite-“ Before his mother could finish, Nate ran up to Yelena, tackled her legs and hugged her fiercely. “Enthusiastic.” Laura finished.

    “Evidently,” Yelena observed, awkwardly. Kate couldn’t help but laugh at the way Yelena’s body stiffened, and Laura could only apologise, but the Russian did her best to shrug it off. She’d faced deadlier foes in her time.

    “Hello Nate,” Yelena said, softly, and gave him a small and gentle pat on the top of his head. The boy looked up into Yelena’s tired eyes. Kate wondered if either of them knew the significance they held in each other’s lives. The child named after her sister, and the sister of his namesake. It was actually all pretty lovely, and neither of them knew why. Kate and Laura exchanged looks, the significance hadn’t escaped the boy’s mother, who looked on, emotion evident in her face.

    Nate grabbed a handful of woollen sweater and pulled. Yelena acquiesced and sank to her haunches to look up into the boy's eyes. “My mom says you’re Kate’s friend, which makes you our friend too. But I’m Kate’s best friend.”

    “Oh really,” Yelena said, her voice low and rasping. “Best friend huh?”

    “Yes!” Nate declared, proudly, as he threw his arms into the air.

    “Quite the title. And we are definitely friends? You and me?” Yelena asked, with narrowed eyes and a smile.

    “Yes, we are definitely friends!”

    The blonde nodded slowly, as if paying careful consideration to his words. “Okay then. As we are friends, I have to tell you a secret.”

    Nate's face lit up with excitement. “What is it?”

    “Well,” Yelena tsked dramatically, and shook her head. “I am not Kate’s friend.”

    The youngest Barton audibly gasped, and Kate smiled warmly. This was everything. Their interaction, Yelena’s tenderness. She felt Laura’s hand find hers, and squeeze gently. She knew, of course she knew. She’d known that Kate was heartbroken as soon as she had walked through the door the day previous. She’d known who had done the breaking the moment Yelena had turned up on their doorstep. And she knew then, that they had managed to piece their love back together that afternoon. Kate squeezed back, because she knew that Laura would keep their secret.

    “What, why aren’t you friends?” Nate asked, clearly shocked by Yelena’s revelation. “Don’t you like her?”

    “Oh, I like her very much,” Yelena whispered, as the fire danced its fickle dance in her dark eyes. “But I’m not her friend, Nate, I’m Kate’s girlfriend.”

    Well, so much for secrets.

    ‘Twas the night before Christmas.

    Chapter Notes It’s me, I’m back! Are you going to get the Christmas Day fluff you deserve? No! Of course not. You’re going to get the Christmas Eve clash of the stubborn bastards that you never asked for. Wooo! But it had to be done.

    Enjoy, and as always… thank you so much!

    The dying embers of the Bartons’ open fire glowed softly into the darkened lounge. Since Nate had been put to bed hours before, the rest of the young-ish contingent hadn’t left their comfortable spots in the lounge. Cooper, Yelena, Kate and Lila had spent the last few hours under the biggest, cosiest blanket whilst they binged The Witcher Season Four. Of course, this meant that Cooper and Yelena had also had to spend the last few hours trying desperately trying to ignore the poorly disguised crushes Kate and Lila held for Henry Cavill.

    The ‘adults’ talked in hushed tones in the kitchen, whilst Kate poured the last few drops of wine from a bottle that her and her girlfriend were sharing, into Yelena’s glass. The blonde smiled her thanks and downed the dregs with aplomb. Her cheeks were alcohol-flushed, and still a little warm from the once raging fire that had been kind enough to gift them its whole heat before burning out.

    Yelena felt relaxed. More relaxed than she had felt in such a long time. Yes, the wine and the company probably had something to do with it, but also, that voice had gone quiet. The voice that had been telling her she wasn’t deserving, that she wasn’t good enough, that she was damaged; at least for the time being, that voice had been extinguished, much like the fire. Her mind felt quieter, more spacious, it felt still. She’d never really realised how wonderful life could be once you stop moving. Once she really stopped to think, she’d been moving since she’d escaped the Red Room’s mind control. It felt good to stop. To be there with the Bartons, these totally, well, not totally, normal people. To laugh and drink and just exist, with Kate’s hand in hers, tucked away under the blankets. It was nice to stop.

    The episode came to a cliff-hanger ending, and despite all of them agreeing that they desperately wanted to know what happened next, three out of the four of them, Yelena not included, agreed that it was important to be in bed before midnight, because you know, Santa. The blonde didn’t have the heart to tell them that Santa wasn’t due until January 7th. So with heavy hearts and even heavier eyes, all four bingers dragged themselves away from the television, said their good nights and began to haul themselves to bed.

    Laura’s hushed whispers emanated from the kitchen, as the Bartons bickered good naturedly. The two kids and Kate didn’t seem too bothered as they started towards the stairs, in ear-shot of the arguing couple. Either small disagreements happened regularly in the Barton household, or the rest of the bedtime contingent simply didn’t hear the mild conflab. Yelena was willing to bet on the latter, considering her sensory perception was far better than most people’s.

    The blonde’s brow furrowed. Laura was asking Clint to leave something alone, and what were the chances that the something was Yelena? The blonde’s frown deepened, she imagined that those chances were quite high, especially as Clint had been doing his best, all evening, to avoid Yelena. Sure, there was already some animosity there that Yelena could understand, layer on top of that the revelation that she was also in a relationship with his ‘adopted’ daughter, and you could turn that animosity up to breaking point. This was always something new she’d have to deal with, it was always something she’d expected, and of course, when his wife had asked him to be agreeable about it, Clint had refused. What a surprise.

    Yelena shook her head and quietly deposited her and Kate’s wine glasses on the dining room table, eager to clean up after herself, but also very much not eager to be noticed by the Bartons, who were still deep in discussion. She hurried away to re-join Kate, who was already half-way up the stairs.

    “Yelena?” Came Clint’s voice from behind her. Shit. She’d been right. Here it was, the talk, their talk. She groaned inwardly. Don’t murder him, don’t murder him, don’t murder him. Yelena knew this had to happen. They would talk and he would be protective. He would tell her to back off, she would tell him she wouldn’t, he would then tell her he would be watching her and then she would tell him that she is always watching him, then it would be over. All Yelena needed to do was suck it up, for one night. She’d done the hard bit; she’d talked to Kate and she’d made things right. She just needed to appease the protective father figure; how hard could it be? All you need to do is act cool.

    Yelena threw a casual, “Hm?” over her shoulder. See, she could do cool, of course she could, but could she do calm? That was yet to be seen.

    “Do you have moment?” Clint asked, but it was never a question for Yelena, not really, she wasn’t going to get any choice. He was really seeking permission from Kate, as his dark eyes flicked to the brunette and then back again to the blonde.

    “I-er...” Was all that Yelena could manage in response. Yep, she was really excelling on the cool front that evening. In fairness to the Russian, she’d already exhausted most of her words for the day. With a slightly troubled brow, she turned to Kate, who smiled and squeezed her hand, gently.

    “You go. I’ll wait up,” she said, softly, with a slightly apologetic look. It seemed as if Kate knew what was on the cards as well. It was something they’d both been afraid of, and something they’d both been avoiding all day, even though they’d both felt his eyes on them. When they’d laughed together, whenever they sat close, when they shared a glass or a blanket or a look, Clint’s ambivalence had been palpable, as had his displeasure. Yelena had no doubt that Clint loved to see Kate happy, and she also knew that if he actually held any real grudge against Yelena, she wouldn’t be welcome in his home, so it was a start. But that didn’t mean that he wasn’t uncomfortable about the whole thing. Oh, Clint Barton was incredibly uncomfortable, and so was Yelena.

    “Good night you two,” Kate said, as she smiled warmly at Laura, and then at Clint.

    “Good night sweetheart,” Laura smiled in return.

    “Good night, Kate,” Clint nodded, with tired eyes.

    Kate offered Yelena one more sympathetic look before she disappeared upstairs, leaving the Russian to her fate. Normally, Yelena might expect a kiss on the cheek to say good night, but not in front of Barton, or anyone else for that matter. She still missed it.

    “I’m going to disappear too,” Laura said as she kissed Clint, softly. “Don’t stay up too late, now.”

    “I won’t,” he responded as a small smile tugged at the corner of his mouth, despite his slightly gruff disposition. They really were rather sweet together, Yelena thought. The way they complimented each other, cared for each other, the way they balanced each other out. Disgusting.

    Laura threw Yelena a small and sympathetic smile, sighed, shook her head, presumably at her husband’s stubborn-headedness, and took herself to bed. And then they were two. For a moment they simply stood, both with the knowledge of what was to come. Yelena’s eyes narrowed out of instinct, they were challenging, assessing him, and they had become more than aware of the poorly concealed bottle that Clint was holding behind his back. She quirked a questioning eyebrow.

    “British vodka? Really?” She asked, clearly unimpressed.

    He shrugged and she got the distinct impression that he really didn’t care about disappointing her. “It’s all I had.”

    Yelena shook her head and smiled, ruefully. “What my sister saw in you, I will never know.” She was teasing and he knew it, but that didn’t mean that it wasn’t a question that she asked herself, regularly.

    “Do you wanna sit?” Clint asked, gesturing to the dining room table.

    “Do I have a choice?” Yelena shot back. She didn’t intend to be defensive, but it was quite quickly becoming her default position. She’d been avoiding this conversation for so long. Now it was here, it came with months' worth of pre-loaded hypotheticals and ‘what ifs’. She knew she was going to be challenged by him, and part of her expected the worst. Expect the worst and hope for the best, surely, he would be kind. Natasha loved him, Kate loved him, even his wife loved him, and she had to be with him every fucking day.

    “Well,” he said as he collected two glasses from the sideboard and placed them on the table, “You could stand but after a few rounds of this you’re gonna wanna sit.” He poured a generous measure into both glasses, slumped down into a chair and gestured for Yelena to join him. After a moment, she did.

    They eyed each other up from across the table as Clint raised his glass.

    “Vzdrognem.” He offered, quietly, with a tip of the glass and a nod of the head. Not bad, Yelena thought, with a smirk. His pronunciation was decent, good even.

    “Vzdrognem,” she offered in return, as she picked up her glass, clinked it satisfyingly against his, and threw her measure back. Clint did the same, and grimaced as the neat alcohol hit the back of his throat. Yelena’s nose only wrinkled; British vodka was too smooth. Tasty but too smooth. Sometimes you just wanted a vodka to kick you in the face and knock you off your feet. That way, you couldn’t feel anything else. This was one of those occasions. But perhaps, by the looks of Clint, anything that could kick Yelena in the face would kick Clint’s head straight off. Perhaps she needed to source something special for next Christmas.

    “So, this is the part of the evening where you tell that if I hurt her there’s an arrow with my name on it right?” Yelena asked, deciding to cut to the chase.

    “Something like that,” he answered, stoically. She frowned ever so slightly, her mouth downturned, and nodded in abject acceptance.

    “Well, if I am going to have to sit through this bullshit, I will need several more of these.” Yelena held her glass out in front of her, and to her surprise, Clint filled it without hesitation. No objection, no smart-ass comment to trump her smart-ass comment. He simply re-filled her glass and then re-filled his. However, in a moment, his second measure was down the hatch. Clint did his best to keep the pain from his features, but his discomfort betrayed him. So, that’s how it going to be. He would match her smart-ass comments with completely dumb displays of dominance which would ultimately lead to his complete and utter downfall, because Yelena could keep this up all night. After all, Ded Moroz wasn’t due till January, and she was pretty sure she was on his naughty list anyway, so Yelena threw the drink back and smiled as the warm liquid raced down the back of her throat.

    Clint placed his glass down on the table, a little too heavily. “So, this is how it’s gonna be, huh?”

    “A testosterone fuelled race to the bottom?”

    He shook his head and sighed. “I don’t think that will solve anything.” What a condescending asshole.

    “What needs solving, Clint?” Yelena asked, sharply, because in her mind there was nothing to solve. There was no problem or conundrum. Nothing needed fixing, and even if her and Kate did still need a little work, it was none of Clint’s business.

    Despite his remonstrations, Clint still re-filled Yelena’s glass, as well as his own. In an irrational need to down hers first, Yelena went to grab her glass but he covered it with his own. “Chase is best as a slow drink,” he said, softer now, clearly thinking it wise to de- escalate the situation. Evidently, both were pretty passionate about Kate Bishop, that was no excuse for things to get out of hand.

    Yelena chewed at the inside of her lip. Russians did not sip vodka, and they certainly didn’t sip British vodka. Clint was lucky she was drinking it at all, but she supposed she had to show some effort to have a dialogue. Drinking together was the first step towards that, and he was obviously trying to get onto her level, however misguided his efforts might have been. She frowned down at the glass in front of her, as he released it from his grasp, and she took it. After moment of final deliberation, she raised it to her lips and sipped. At least it was cold.

    There was a moment of silence as Yelena placed the glass back down on the table and sighed loudly. Get it done, Yelena. Just grit your teeth and tear it off like a band-aid. Not that Yelena, was afraid of tearing off band-aids, oh no. She was terrified of it.

    Yelena looked up to meet Clint’s eyes. His jaw was tight and his body tense. He was enjoying this about as much as she was. Yelena took some comfort in that.

    “Whatever it is that you need to say, or ask, we do it now and then it is done, da?”

    Clint’s eyes wandered in deliberation, as he took a thoughtful sip of his vodka. Pussy. After a moment longer he nodded his acceptance. “Sure, okay.”

    “Okay, so ask,” Yelena said, with another sip of her Chase. Her nose wrinkled once more, as she was determined not to like it.

    “How long’s it been?” He asked. Starting small, wise. Yelena could deal with small.

    “Just over two months,” she replied.

    “But you’ve been living with her?” That question was a little more pointed, and its implications were clear. She and Kate hadn’t been just a two-month thing, which was true, to an extent. She and Kate had been a thing since the moment they’d met, whatever that thing was.

    Yelena nodded, thoughtfully. “Since I came to S.H.I.E.L.D.”

    Something flickered in his eyes. Was it hurt? “She didn’t tell me.” He sounded disappointed; he probably was.

    The Russian shrugged. “She was worried about what you would say.”

    “Yelena, don’t give me that,” he snapped, disbelievingly. The idea that Kate was afraid of Clint and his opinions was not a palatable one for Barton to swallow. But swallow it he would have to, along with some of his pride, perhaps.

    “She cares very much about what you think of her,” Yelena offered, and it was true. Everyone knew it. Clint Barton’s opinion and approval was the most important thing in Kate’s life. It went far beyond what she sought from her mother, or her mother’s ‘friends’, or Yelena even.

    “Do S.H.I.E.L.D. know?” He asked, with a change of tack.

    The blonde frowned and shook her head. The idea of telling S.H.I.E.L.D. was one of those, ‘if we don’t talk about it, it doesn’t exist’, problems. Of course, now she and Kate were talking more, it would probably be something they would have to address, eventually. Yelena wasn’t looking forward to it, but if worst came to worst, at least she’d have an excuse to punch Carol in the face.

    “Does anyone there know?”

    “Nope. You are the first, congratulations.” She said, trying but failing to keep the facetious smile from her face.

    “Why haven’t you told them?” Clint seemed surprised, as if declaring an intra-work relationship to your work colleagues was the easiest thing in the world, as if it was their right to know. Kate and Yelena had already put enough pressure on their relationship by themselves, they didn’t need the scrutiny of S.H.I.E.L.D. upon them, and she certainly didn’t feel as if she owed an American Government agency anything above what was in her remit as an employee. Was falling into a non-sexy but incredibly romantic bed with my charge part of my remit? Maybe don’t mention that part.

    Instead, Yelena simply feigned nonchalance. “It’s my business.”

    “First of all,” Clint shifted forward in his seat and his eyes flashed in annoyance. “It’s not just your business. You’re a couple and you’re going to have to get used to make decisions together.” That, they could agree on. “Second of all, your relationship could compromise a mission. You need to declare it.” That, they would not agree on.

    “I’m not going to let her get hurt,” Yelena tried to dismiss his concern and took another healthy sip of her vodka. Yelena’s top priority was always to protect Kate, sometimes from Kate herself.

    Unfortunately for Yelena, Clint’s concerns couldn’t be dismissed so easily. “Your relationship could also compromise the people around you, or the people you’re supposed to be helping. What would you do, if it were Kate or,” he waved his hands around in front of him, momentarily, trying to conjure up an example that would do his pathetic hypothetical situation justice. “…Five civilians?”

    Was he kidding? Five civilians? This was too easy. “Kate.”

    “Okay, Kate or the occupants of an apartment complex?”

    “Kate.”

    Clint looked at her in disbelief. “You don’t truly expect me to believe that?”

    Yelena shrugged. It was Kate, it really was that simple. It was always Kate, it would never not be Kate, and if he struggled to understand that, this entire conversation was a complete waste of time, and Yelena was beyond tired. In fact, she’d been up for nearly forty hours, and Clint was really starting to take the proverbial piss.

    “This has been great,” She smiled a saccharine smile that didn’t reach her eyes as she got to her feet, causing her chair to scrape loudly across the floor. “Thank you for the overpriced vodka.” She didn’t mean it, but she certainly felt it in her legs.

    In an instant, Clint’s hand was gripped, tightly, around Yelena’s forearm and she had to bite back the instinct to break it. “We are not done,” he said, quietly. It wasn’t aggressive, it was measured and factual.

    Yelena’s skin as practically crawling, she wanted to punch him so bad. How was he doing this too her? How was he so..., he was just so... oh, no, I like him.

    The Russian yanked her arm from his grasp, and shivered, inwardly. Gross. “Are you going to sit back down, or am I going to have to make you?” And now he was joking about fighting, please stop.

    A sarcastic, “Ha,” was all that she could muster, as she slumped back down into her chair, refilled her glass and began to sip. SIP! What had he done to her? In such a short space of time.

    “What happens to Kate, if she has to choose between you and the mission?” It was an interesting question for sure, but one that Yelena had never doubted the answer of. Kate genuinely cared; it was why she did what she did. And of course, she was willing to make sacrifices of her own, she was willing to put the needs of others before her own, so Yelena had always assumed she would make the hard decisions, but Yelena had also seen how her girlfriend had been when the harsh realities of life of as an Avenger had come calling. “She’s not like you, Yelena, she can’t turn a blind eye.”

    Yelena laughed a small, indignant laugh. He really thought that little of her. Suddenly, she cared what he thought, and she didn’t like it. “You think I don’t care about the deaths of others?”

    “I don’t think they weigh on you,” he explained matter-of-factly, “I don’t think you carry them around with you.”

    “What, like you?” Yelena laughed again, with more venom this time. The people this man had killed, and here he was, accusing her of being uncaring, of being inhuman.

    But all Clint did was shake his head, sadly. “We’re more alike than I like to admit, Yelena, but you know that.”

    She certainly did. They were both killers, a hundred times over. They’d both killed in the line of duty, but they’d also both killed seeking vengeance. Yelena would have killed him, she wanted to kill him, she wanted someone to blame for Natasha, and he wouldn’t have been the first person she had killed over her sister. She had been so angry after her death, killing seemed to be the only option. It’s why she became a paid assassin in the first place, and of course, she wasn’t going to lie to herself, the killing had felt good, at first. She hadn’t told Kate that, she hadn’t told anyone. Maybe she never could, or maybe one day, she could at least tell the Ronin. Maybe one day.

    “So, what are you saying, that I am no good for her?” Yelena asked. “I think Kate can make those kinds of decisions for herself.”

    “Is that why she stepped off that flight looking like a ghost yesterday?” If it were possible, Clint was growing even more protective.

    Yelena swallowed. “She knew what she was getting into,” The Russian said, dismissively. But had she? Had Kate known? Had she really known that Yelena was this dysfunctional? Had she known about her sexuality, about the compromises she would have to make to have a relationship that she cherished? Yelena could feel herself getting defensive again, but she needed to shake it off, otherwise they would never get through this conversation. The only problem was, it didn’t feel like a conversation, it felt like an accusation, an attack, on her and her relationship with Kate.

    “And what is that exactly?” His eyes narrowed and his features darkened.

    “I think you probably know, better than most,” And it was true, which was kind of what made their entire conversation ridiculous. He knew who she was, because he loved her sister. He knew how damaged she was, because he loved her sister. He knew her past, because he helped her sister escape it, literally and figuratively.

    “Do I?”

    “Sure,” she nodded, casually, as if it were obvious. “Severe childhood trauma resulting in a maladaptive, dismissive-avoidant attachment style. Distrustful and fearful of rejection with dissociative episodes. You know, the standard Red Room fare.” She was being flippant and it was making him uncomfortable.

    He sighed and pinched the bridge of his nose. “She is too-”

    “Too what?” Yelena interjected, aggressively. Her temper had been well and truly stoked. “Too good for me? Too happy and normal for me?” Of course he thought that, of course he did. Yelena wanted to rescind every nice thought she’d ever had about Clint Barton. She did not like him, she did not like his taste in alcohol, and she certainly did not want to confide in him about how much she’d enjoyed killing people after Natasha’s death.

    Clint held his hands up in repentance in an attempt to quickly de-escalate the situation. “That wasn’t what I was going to say.”

    Whatever. Yelena’s jaw twitched in irritation. “Then what was it?” She asked, through gritted teeth.

    Silence fell over the Bartons’ open plan kitchen/diner. Yelena could tell that Clint was weighing up his next words, carefully. Yelena could only imagine what kind of bullshit what going to come out of his mouth next.

    Finally, he sighed and said, “She’s a kid, Yelena, you’re not.”

    And what absolute bullshit it was. “Wow. Okay.” Wow. The Russian was done sipping. She threw back her vodka with relish, she was done taking this. “Firstly, I was born six years ago, when I got out of the Red Room.” Clint went to speak but Yelena cut him off before he had even managed a breath. “Secondly, she is way more mature than me, on every level. Thirdly,” she said, with a no-bullshit smile, “How old is your wife?”

    “We’re not talking about me.” She’d made him uncomfortable, good. Long may it continue, and so she did.

    “Look, I get it. You are worried I am going to hurt her. You are worried I am going to put her in danger. So am I. That is why…” Yelena sighed loudly in frustration. “That is why she turned up here looking like a ghost, because I hurt her. I hurt her because I was afraid of hurting her. Do you know how fucking stupid that is?” Fuck she was so angry. So angry at herself for being such a fucking idiot, so angry at Clint for being such a proud and protective asshole and so angry that he was smiling at her. Goddam smiling!

    “I really do,” he nodded. “I think it’s really fucking stupid.”

    If Yelena thought things couldn’t get any worse, they did, because all of a sudden, she was smiling. Now, she just wanted to punch herself in the face, she was beyond caring about causing him physical harm. She just needed to be put out of her misery.

    “Do you worry you might hurt her again?” He asked, softer this time. Yep, just murder me.

    “I don’t plan on it,” she shrugged. He gave her a look that said, you’re gonna have to do better than that. “I’m actively trying to avoid it.”

    “You know what will happen if you do, right?”

    “You are going to kick my ass?”

    “Absolutely,” he said, resolutely, as if it were fact. It was not fact.

    Yelena laughed, good naturedly. Who was this man? “Good luck with that.”

    “You haven’t seen all my best moves yet,” he teased, whilst taking a sip of his Chase.

    “You were holding back?” She asked, sceptically.

    “I think that was pretty obvious.”

    “How noble of you, Clint Barton, government agent, hero, merciful Avenger.” She rolled her eyes and poured herself some more vodka. Yelena was hoping that if she drank enough, she wouldn’t remember any of this conversation. If Christmas was a write off, she’d always have another go at it in two weeks' time.

    “You know, you’re more like her than you think?” He smiled, sentimentally and Yelena quirked an eyebrow.

    “So, capable of love then? Deserving of it even? Despite the brainwashing, despite the trauma, despite the baggage?”

    “Of course,” he said earnestly. So, it was time for some honesty of her own.

    “Well then, to answer your question from earlier, if I had to choose between Kate and an apartment building or Kate and New York City or Kate and the world? I would choose me.”

    Clint’s face changed. He grew sad for a moment and he couldn’t meet her gaze. He simply played with the vodka in his glass, his eyes fixated on the swirling liquid that left inky trails along the inside of the crystal. Yelena knew exactly who he was thinking about.

    “Did Kate tell you that we named Nate after her?” He asked quietly, after a moment of further contemplation.

    “I did not know that,” Yelena said, solemnly. She smiled slightly at the notion. Nat would have loved that, she would have found it corny for sure, but she would have loved it all the same. Plus, he seemed to be a good kid, if not a little boisterous, but what kid his age wasn’t? They would have got on well. Yelena wondered how much Nate ever got to see of her sister, did he know her? Had he had more time with her than she had? She supposed it was only right, they were her family too.

    “We thought he was going to be a girl at first,” Clint explained, and he smiled, ruefully to himself. “Nat was so excited, but Nate was never a disappointment of course. She loved him…” His voice trailed off and his smile faded. “And then we lost him, and Cooper, and Lila, and Laura.”

    To have lost so many must have been difficult, but to lose your entire family, to lose your entire identity, the people who made you whole and you, it must have been unbearable. Yelena looked around the room. The house that was so full of life and warmth, so full of love, must have felt so empty. Of course, Yelena hadn’t exactly been around either, she hadn’t been anywhere in fact. She couldn't have known how her parents had dealt with the loss of her, how they’d felt, not until she came home to discover a life without Natasha. They’d traded one daughter for the other. It had been such a tragic mixture of pure unadulterated delight and despair. Yelena knew that her parents would never fully recover, and she also knew that, deep down, she would never fully feel at peace knowing it was she who survived and not her sister.

    Yelena took Clint in. He must have been a broken man, and yet he’d put himself back together. Even getting his family back couldn’t have fixed the damage done, couldn’t have made the grief go away. You can’t reverse that, not fully. So, all she could say was, “I’m sorry,” which felt pretty useless, but at least she meant it.

    He shook his head and took another sip. “Don’t be sorry. You went too, right?”

    She nodded, slowly. “I did. The first thing I did when I came back was try to find Natasha,” she took a pause as a sudden wave of emotion threatened to get the better of her. “By the time I did, you had put her in the ground.”

    “I’m sorry for that.” He started, but that’s not what she had meant. It hurt, but she wasn’t angry, not anymore.

    “Don’t be,” she smiled, “You were the one who put ‘sister’ on her gravestone weren’t you?”

    Clint nodded, confirming what she’d known since last Christmas. When he’d told her that Natasha spoke of her to him, she’d known, and she was grateful.

    “Thank you,” she said, honestly, her cheeks now flushed. There had been a little too much vodka consumed a little too quickly, and perhaps there was a little too much emotion weighing heavy in the room as well.

    He shrugged, as if it were the most obvious thing he could have done, that it wasn’t even for him to question whether it should have been there. “She loved you,” he said, simply.

    Yelena’s heart tightened and she had to smile to stop herself from crying. Natasha’s death would never not be painful. Yelena had lived her life not in control of her own destiny. She thought she’d finally wrestled it back, only to have that control taken away again when she vanished. She wasn't even given the chance to save her sister, she wasn’t given a choice, Natasha was simply taken away. “I still love her, very much,” she whispered.

    “I know,” he said softly. It was weird to think about really, that Yelena was now the Black Widow spending Christmas with the Bartons, not Natasha. Weird to think that the events of the last few years had led to this.

    Yelena had always wondered what family was good enough to take Natasha away from her. Of course, it was always an irrational thought, it was never that Natasha had loved another family more than her, another sibling more than her, a sibling like Clint. No, it was her fear that had kept her away. But now, here they were. Sibling and sibling, around the table, and perhaps soon to be under it, at American Christmas. Yelena wondered what Nat would have thought of this, would she have been the one to have this conversation with her? Or would she have been kicking Clint’s ass for even trying to broach the subject? Yelena smiled to herself at the thought of Natasha kicking Clint’s ass on a cold Christmas Eve. It was a good thought.

    “Did you know that Christmas is a pretty new thing in Russia?” Yelena asked, her mind now thinking back to the Christmases she had spent with Nat.

    Clint nodded, warmly. “I did know that.”

    “My parents never really had any traditions of their own but when we were over here, in Ohio, we had to do our best to fit in. We went to church every Sunday, like the rest of the community, and each year we would have to be part of the Christmas pageant. Do you have them here?”

    “Oh yeah, Nate kicked ass this year as Innkeeper Number Two.”

    “Wow, that is quite the role. Very important in the story, can you imagine if he had said yes?”

    “I don’t even want to think about it.” Yelena couldn’t help but grin. Clint was funny. This was awful, but like, in a good way.

    “Natasha was too old for all that stuff,” Yelena continued, “And she was way too cool for it anyways. Man, she was so cool,” she said with a wistful sigh. “I however, was not cool. I had no chill when it came to the Christmas pageant. Every year, I wanted to be Mary. Every year. The last Christmas that we were in the States for, I was cast as Mary’s alternate. Can you imagine the insult? An alternate.” Vodka threatened to slosh from Yelena’s glass as she gesticulated passionately. She was still angry, after all these years.

    Clint could only laugh. “I pity your parents.”

    “Do not pity them,” Yelena warned playfully. “They were awful people. Still are. I love them, but...awful sometimes.”

    “To raise you, can’t be,” Clint countered, his voice dripping with sarcasm.

    “I am going to ignore that heinous slight on my character and continue with my story, if that’s okay with you?”

    “It’s going somewhere, right?”

    “Fuck you,” she said, amiably, as she took a generous gulp of her vodka. “And fuck this sipping thing.”

    After another top-up and another gulp, Yelena continued her story. “So, remember, I was Mary’s alternate, and on the day of the pageant, I show up but there is no Mary to be found. We wait and we wait. I am putting my angel costume on; I make a very beautiful angel by the way.”

    “You have a lot of angelic qualities.” Sarcastic bastard.

    “I get told this a lot. So, we are waiting and waiting but Abigail Jensen never shows.” Yelena hated Abigail Jensen. Not only was she perfect in every way, she also had a portable CD player, that she ONLY listened to worship music on. What a waste.

    “So, you got to play Mary?” Clint asked, clearly hooked on Yelena’s story. She was a great storyteller, after all, so it kind of went without saying.

    “Totally.” She threw her hands up in mini celebration. “Worst decision ever, I was awful, tanked it, but Abigail Jensen learned a valuable lesson that day.”

    “And what was that?” Clint asked, with a smile.

    Yelena threw back the rest of her vodka and slammed her glass down on the table. “That Natasha Romanoff did not learn how to tie knots at Girl Scouts.”

    Clint was laughing now, genuinely laughing. His eyes danced in the light of the still lit Christmas tree and his smile was brighter than she had ever seen it. And here she was, thinking he was a grumpy asshole twenty-four seven, three-hundred and sixty-five days a year.

    “No, she did not,” he agreed, wholeheartedly. Natasha Romanoff was incredibly good with ropes, and getting out of them. Sadly, for Abigail Jensen, and the rest of the congregation, the first choice Mary was not.

    “Why are you telling me this?” he asked. It was the least loaded question he’d asked her all evening.

    Yelena simply shrugged as if it were obvious. “That has always been my favourite Christmas memory.”

    “Despite tanking?”

    “Hell yes,” she said, fervently. “But do you know what my second favourite Christmas memory is?” Clint shrugged; he clearly had no idea, but then again, why would he? Even if he was there for it.

    Yelena thought back to the biting wind, the dark rooftop, the adrenaline from the fight rushing through her veins. Her life changed day that, and so much for the better. She smiled, thankful that she could reminisce without heartache, thankful that she had fixed things with Kate, with the woman that she knew she loved, deep down she knew. Even if she wasn’t ready to admit it, not even to herself, and even if she wasn’t ready to accept what it all really meant. “Meeting Kate Bishop up on that roof, that is my second favourite Christmas memory,” she said, honestly and openly.

    “She had a shot on you, you know that right?”

    Yelena nodded, solemnly. “I know.”

    Clint smiled; it was funny how things worked out sometimes. “There’s no way she was taking you down up there though,” he added.

    “Oh no,” Yelena said, quickly. There was no way. "But it is the thought that counts, right?”

    “Sure, whatever you say.” Clint was drunk, and flushed, and very amused. He was a sweet drunk. Angry when sober, but sweet when not. It turned out; Yelena was a sentimental drunk.

    “If you could see her now, Clint. She has come so far in such a short amount of time. She does not need my protection, or yours.” Yelena knew this wasn’t how she felt, she knew she wanted to protect Kate, knew she felt compelled to, but she also knew that Kate was at a jumping off point. She was ready to be a true Avenger, not just an Avenger with training wheels. She just needed to stop asking people to stab her.

    “It’s my job to look out for her,” he mumbled stubbornly.

    “That’s actually my job,” Yelena asserted, and she wasn’t wrong, so Clint simply decided to tease her instead of concede.

    “How’s that working out for you?”

    “Up until two nights ago, I’d say pretty well.”

    He nodded in agreement. Somehow, after drinking and arguing and almost fighting, then drinking some more and almost crying, and then drinking even more and pretty much only laughing, Yelena and Clint had managed to land upon the very same page. “You will need to tell S.H.I.E.L.D, eventually. Sooner rather than later.” Clint warned, but this time, he wasn’t being antagonistic, he was being caring.

    “I know,” Yelena sighed. She paused for a moment, her brow furrowed. “Are you going to say something, if we don’t?” She asked, a little apprehensively.

    He met her eyes. “No,” he said, “But I’ll be very disappointed.” She believed that. “And it’ll be Laura lecturing you next time, not me.”

    Yelena scoffed. “Okay Barton, I think I can handle that.”

    “You think so?” He asked, in surprise as he pointed to his chest, “I’m good cop.”

    “Alright, alright,” she held her hands up in surrender as she rose from her chair, a little unsteadily. Fuck you British vodka. It was late, she was drunk, and there nothing she wanted more than to be held close by her Kate Bishop. Of course, Kate would tell her that she stank of alcohol, but that would simply mean that she got to be little spoon which, despite her passionate outward protestations, was in fact something she secretly quite enjoyed.

    “Consider yourself warned, Yelena,” Clint said, as he got to his feet, clearly feeling the effects of the alcohol.

    “What are you going to do if I break all your rules, Clint Barton? What are you gonna do if I hurt her? Fight me?” She asked, with a drunken smile.

    “Do you really need an incentive not to?” He countered, much to her enjoyment.

    “Not really, no. I want to make her happy. I care for her, more than I ever thought possible. She makes me feel things that I never thought were possible, for me anyways. Do you know what that is like?”

    He smiled to himself, and Yelena could see the love that Clint held for his wife and his family, evident in his eyes. “I do.”

    Born in different decades, to different families on different continents, and yet they could still find more than one point of common ground. Their love for their sister, and their love for the wilfully passionate women in their lives. Yelena resolved herself, as she knew Clint would understand.

    “Then please do not judge me upon my mistakes?” Yelena asked. “Let me show you how good we are, together. Maybe I will end up hurting her, maybe this is a ridiculously dumb experiment and all I will end up proving is that Red Room girls are irreparably broken. But maybe, just maybe, it is going to work, and I am going to work my hardest to see that it does.”

    Clint blinked, as his alcohol fogged brain fought to fully comprehend her statement.

    “Okay then,” he managed, with a nod.

    “Okay then,” Yelena responded in turn.

    “The threat of violence still stands though,” he warned as he cleared the glasses from the table.

    “Pfft, I am always up for a fight.”

    Clint walked the glasses over and deposited them in the sink. Even rinsing seemed too much work for that time of night, after that much vodka. “It’s agreed then,” he said, matter-of- factly, as he turned to Yelena and offered her his hand. The Russian scrutinised it for a moment, she could count the number of times in her life she’d shaken someone’s hand on... well, one hand. It wasn’t something she’d often do, as any gentleman’s agreement had to be honoured, and, up until recently, Yelena hadn’t exactly been a woman of honour.

    After a moment’s further deliberation, Yelena took Clint’s hand in hers and shook it, as she narrowed her eyes in faux scepticism. “It’s agreed,” she said, before she headed back to the dining room table and relieved it of its vodka bottle.

    “This is mine now, right?”

    “I thought you said it was overpriced?” He teased, amicably, but he had no intention of letting her have the bottle.

    “That does not mean it is not drinkable,” Yelena argued, and it was totally true, for Yelena had drunk a lot of it.

    “Give it back, please?” Clint asked, in his best parent to child voice. Yelena frowned; she didn’t feel like it. She was Russian, surely the vodka was hers by right. “Yelena,” Clints chided, his tone now more severe, “Give it back.” It was not a question.

    Yelena huffed and rolled her eyes. Fine, she would just drink it all the next day anyways. Christmas was only fit for one thing, which was drinking, heavily.

    “Whatever’s left, you can take back with you,” he reasoned as he stuck the bottle back in the freezer. Yelena ‘hmphed’, it was a reasonable offer, but she wasn’t going to let him know that.

    “I have to spend another day with you. There will be none left!”

    Clint let out a small laugh and shook his head disbelievingly as he passed her, and started his way up the stairs and to his bed.

    “What?” she asked.

    He stopped on the bottom stair to turn and face her. “You’re funny,” he simply said.

    “You’re not,” she quipped and he scoffed again. What he meant to say was ‘you’re hilarious’, Yelena was sure of it.

    They both stood for a moment, eyes tired and their brains failing them. Maybe sipping had been a good idea after all. Any more shots and Yelena might never have made it from the table.

    “Good night, Yelena,” Clint said, quietly, and then checked his watch. His eyes lit up, warmly. “And Happy Christmas.”

    “Happy Christmas, Clint,” Yelena said, softly. A small smile pulled at the corner of her lips. Maybe they really could have a happy Christmas, after all. All of them, together. Who’d have predicted it?
